newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - "Russia's Murdoch" Gusinsky wants money, not power.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - "Russia's Murdoch" Gusinsky wants money, not power.

text.p: Vladimir Gusinsky, whose Media-Most group is Russia's first media empire, welcomes comparisons with Australian-born magnate Rupert Murdoch but denies he sees his growing business as a political power base.
"Murdoch and Time-Warner are great examples," said 44-year-old Gusinsky in an interview. "I would like to match them in size -- this is my yardstick."

Gusinsky, whose recent move to concentrate on his media investments fuelled speculation that his goal is political power, says there is a limit to the lessons to be learned from Murdoch's News Corp and Time-Warner of the United States.
"We are following foreign structures. But Russia is a different country...with a different market, a different way of thinking."

Gusinsky is one of the most controversial -- and reportedly richest -- men in Russia. Everything he has touched has turned to gold. In Soviet times, he studied the oil industry, was a theatre director and drove a private taxi.
He launched his first company during Mikhail Gorbachev's "perestroika" reforms in 1986 and three years later started building his Most empire. The name means "bridge".
The group now includes one of Russia's biggest banks.

Russian media speculate that Gusinsky bankrolled powerful Moscow Mayor Yuri Luzhkov for a time. He clashed with President Boris Yeltsin's then chief bodyguard Alexander Korzhakov, seen as a hawkish power behind the Kremlin throne.
DENIES POLITICAL AMBITIONS
According to some reports, he has since moved on from city politics to the national arena.

Gusinsky was cited as one of seven Russian tycoons who helped tip the scales against a communist comeback by throwing their cash behind Yeltsin for a second term and drafted Anatoly Chubais, now Kremlin chief-of-staff, to run his campaign.
Opinion polls regularly name him in the top five most influential businessmen in Russia. But Gusinsky says he is just a successful businessman and nothing more.

"A secretary to a top official has more clout than me," Gusinsky told Reuters, sitting in his plush office on the executive floor of the Most Group in central Moscow -- which shares a building with Mayor Luzhkov.

Dismissing reports that he says are being paid for by opponents or ordered by his enemies in the secret service, he said he had decided to concentrate on the media because he wanted to make money, not increase his political influence.
"For us, mass media is a way of making money, good money."
GROWING INTEREST IN MEDIA
Much of Russia's big business has shown a growing interest in the media and has been snapping up stakes in television, newspapers and magazines.
Gusinsky moved more boldly and in January quit as the head of Most Bank and Most Group to concentrate on Media Most.

"The main difference is that many enterpreneurs invest in the mass media to increase their influence while we view it as business," he said. "We deal with it openly while they use it as a system of influence and to hide who owns what."

Media Most includes the popular television channel NTV, with an audience of 120 million, and the new satellite system NTV-Plus which has four channels -- two movie, one music and one sport. A planned news channel is on hold.
NTV-Plus, launched this year, has more than 30,000 suscribers.

The media empire also includes the big-selling weekly TV guide Sem Dney (Seven Days), the heavyweight liberal daily Sevodnya and Itogi (Results) a glossy news weekly produced jointly with the Washington Post's Newsweek and the first of its type in Russia.
It also has a book publishing house and Ekho Moskvy, a local Moscow radio station with strong following among liberals.
Gusinsky declined to give any figures but said he had a controlling stake in Media Most, which in its turn has between 52 and 100 percent of each component of the group.
TELEVISION IS THE JEWEL IN THE CROWN
Gusinsky sees television as the jewel in his empire's crown and pins huge hopes on it. His plans are ambitious.
Five-year-old NTV is already profitable but all revenues are reinvested in the company, he said.
NTV will have its third Western audit in 1997. It will go public next year and seek a share listing. Gusinsky said it is likely to be listed in the United States.
"We will be an absolutely transparent company," he said. "We understand perfectly well that the media business should be in an open market."
NTV Plus which is selling about 250 receiving sets a day at present, will expand to produce more channels, Gusinsky said.

A television production centre is being set up and Gusinsky also buys films abroad to show them on television and sell on video -- striking a heavy blow, he said, against Russia's huge industry producing poor-quality pirate copies.

But his appetite seems insatiable. With the Russian film industry a shadow of what is used to be in the Soviet days, Media-Most is financing the production of 10 films this year and developing its own network of cinemas.
Gusinsky insists his editors and producers are free to put out what they wish and says he would intervene only if their policies caused financial losses.
"I think every business starts with a feeling. It is a very creative process. When you've got this feeling, you put it into calculation, infrastructure and so on," he said.

"After all the documents are ready, comes the second stage -- moving rapidly ahead. At this stage the main thing is to ignore outside signals, to ignore any new information, positive or negative. Once you set your goal, you must become a rhino and never stop on the way."
